slides.title: Connector C: keep it, redesign it, and decide on a sunset with evidence

paragraphs.text: Connector C: keep it, redesign it, and decide on a sunset with evidence
Should Vesper MedTech discontinue sterile connector C and redeploy the team to connector D?
Vesper MedTech
Board of directors
Board discussion document. Synthetic benchmark data
Executive summary
Keep connector C and redesign it: exit in 2027 would cost $4.75M–5.5M in year one and break the board's cash and bundle limits
C's 8.3% reported margin is an allocation effect; on direct contribution it is Vesper's most profitable connector
–	Only $0.4M of the $3.3M charged to C would go with it
–	C earns 63% direct contribution margin, against 50% for D
Exit would cost $5.5M in year one and $3.4M a year after, and it breaks the cash and bundle limits
–	Moving C customers to D wins back at most $750K a year
–	Penalties of $2.1M are 2.3 times the 2027 cash limit
The case against C is not proven: the renewal gap reflects who buys C, and the service gap is in bundles
–	C buyers are smaller, older-equipment, lower-coverage accounts
–	Bundle fill is 91% against 95% required; the dashboard hides it
Redesign C now, renew both bundles with 2029 exit terms, and decide on a sunset in 2028
–	Redesign alone adds contribution within the cash limit
–	It pays back in a year if savings reach 44% of the estimate

slides.title: The renewal gap of 9 percentage points shows who buys C; it does not prove that C drives customers away

paragraphs.text: 1 Economics    2 Exit cost    3 Evidence    4 Plan
The renewal gap of 9 percentage points shows who buys C; it does not prove that C drives customers away
The claim rests on a snapshot, not a test
C buyers differ in ways that predict churn on their own
Before acting on it, test it like for like
▪	The CEO's scatter plot compares hospital renewal rates by product mix
▪	It shows that C accounts renew less often, not why
▪	No account in the sample is seen before and after a change in C
▪	Smaller hospitals buy C disproportionately
▪	C is concentrated in accounts running legacy equipment
▪	C accounts get lower customer-success coverage
▪	Each of these can lower renewal whether or not C is in the order
▪	Compare C and non-C accounts of the same size, equipment and coverage
▪	Track renewal where coverage rises but C stays
▪	Until then, read the gap as a coverage signal, not a product verdict
▪	The evidence neither proves nor rules out a C effect
